result.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): A sets almost every question in a real situation on the floor, its wrong options are mostly plausible, and it explains every option, which fits the rubric much better. It does add some guidance that isn't on the supplied list (tell the supervisor, offer to walk with the coworker, repairs aren't part of the check), its explanation of the walking-pace option in Q2 is confusing, and it leaves placeholders like [weight] and [distance] in the questions. B sticks closely to the list and covers every topic, but most of its questions just ask for a recited rule or number, several wrong options are filler (turn off your lights, tire pressure, operate only in the freezer), and its answer key never says why the tempting wrong answer is wrong. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B frames nearly every question as a floor situation, has plausible wrong options, and explains each one, which is what the rubric asks for. B does add some content not in the session: telling a supervisor about overloads, the center-of-gravity and scraping explanations, waiting until the pedestrian has cleared, and calling walking pace 'not a site standard'. It also leaves bracketed placeholders to fill in and has an awkward stem in Q1. A sticks strictly to the session list and covers every topic, but it is mostly recall questions, includes filler options such as 'turn off your lights' and 'recommended tire pressure', and its key only restates the rule without explaining why the wrong answers fail.
